title: Alaska's Glaciers Are Melting Way Faster Than We Thought—Here's the 3-Week Surprise
summary: What if turning up the thermostat by just one degree made your ice cream melt three weeks faster? That's exactly what's happening to Alaska's glaciers! Scientists used special radar satellites to peek through clouds and darkness, watching over 3,000 glaciers from space. They found a startling pattern: for every 1°C rise in average summer temperature, the melt season stretches by about three extra weeks. That's a lot more time for ice to vanish. The radar, called SAR, works like a super-powered camera that doesn't need sunlight. It bounces microwave pulses off the ice and catches the echoes. This let researchers count 'melt days'—days when the whole glacier surface is slushy. They also discovered that short heat waves can be brutal. During unusually warm spells, glaciers lost up to 28% more of the snow that normally shields them from the sun. That snow is like a protective blanket; without it, the ice underneath melts even faster. One scientist said this helps us predict how much ice will disappear in a warmer future. Since Alaska's glaciers are a big source of sea-level rise, knowing this is super important. The study was published in Nature and used data from Europe's Sentinel-1 satellites, which zip over every 12 days. Next time you hear about a heat wave, think of those glaciers sweating it out!
why_it_matters: The extra water from melting glaciers can cause floods in coastal areas, which might affect beaches and cities that kids might visit or live in.

background_read: Alaska contains thousands of glaciers, more than anywhere else in the United States. As the planet warms, these huge rivers of ice are shrinking rapidly.
The Sentinel-1 satellites, part of Europe's Copernicus program, can monitor glaciers day and night, even through thick clouds, using radar technology.
Scientists have long known that melting glaciers add water to the oceans, but this study shows just how sensitive they are to even small temperature increases.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists and researchers studying glacier melt from space.
WHAT: They discovered that each 1°C rise lengthens the melt season by about three weeks, and heat waves strip away 28% more of the protective snow layer.
WHERE: Over 3,000 glaciers across Alaska, measured by radar satellites orbiting Earth.
WHY: To improve predictions of future sea-level rise and understand how fast glaciers will disappear in a warmer world.

perspectives.description: This research helps communities prepare for rising seas, giving them time to build defenses and plan for the future.
The findings are alarming because they show even small temperature increases cause big changes, making it harder to stop glacier loss.
The study highlights how advanced satellites are revolutionizing our understanding of climate change, giving us more accurate data than ever before.
